summary: This informational guide describes how IETF meetings and working groups work, discusses related organizations, and introduces the standards process. It is not a formal process document. It replaced RFC 3160 and was itself replaced by RFC 6722.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a friendly guidebook for newcomers to the group that writes internet rules, explaining how its meetings work and how ideas become standards.

subtitle: A guide to how the IETF works, its meetings, and the standards process

tldr.problem: The IETF has grown into a large, complex organization that newcomers find difficult to navigate, with unclear processes and procedures for participation.
tldr.mechanism: This informational RFC explains the inner workings of IETF meetings and Working Groups, describes related organizations like the IAB and IESG, and introduces how the standards process works, providing practical guidance for newcomers.
tldr.outcome: The document was superseded by RFC 6722, but it remains a valuable reference for understanding how the IETF operates and how to participate effectively in standards development.

today: RFC 4677 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 6722. The fundamental principles of IETF operations described here remain largely valid, though specific details about tools, areas, and processes have evolved. The document stands as a historical reference to how the IETF was documented and understood in 2006.

sections.title: Introduction and IETF Basics
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force is a loosely self-organized group of people who contribute to the engineering and evolution of Internet technologies. It is the principal body engaged in developing new Internet standard specifications. The IETF is unique: it has no formal membership, no board of directors, and no dues. Anyone can attend meetings or participate on mailing lists. The IETF operates on the principle of rough consensus and running code, meaning decisions are made through broad agreement rather than formal voting, and specifications must be implementable and implemented.

The IETF is not a conference, trade show, or traditional standards organization. It is a community of volunteers—network designers, operators, vendors, researchers, and others—who meet three times a year to advance the Internet. Newcomers often experience culture shock; most attendees wear casual clothing, wireless laptops abound in sessions, and the atmosphere is deliberately informal and technically focused.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is a group of volunteers from all over who work on Internet standards. Nobody owns it, nobody votes formally, and anyone can join. They meet three times a year to discuss and develop technical specifications.

sections.title: The Organizations Behind the IETF
sections.content:
The IETF's structure is provided by several related organizations. The Internet Society (ISOC) is a non-profit membership organization that provides financial and legal support, insurance coverage, and public relations. ISOC also hosts the IETF's administrative support infrastructure.

The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) is responsible for technical management of IETF activities and the standards process. It consists of Area Directors from eight technical areas (Applications, General, Internet, Operations and Management, Real-time Applications and Infrastructure, Routing, Security, and Transport), selected by a Nominations Committee and appointed for two-year terms.

The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) oversees the big picture of the Internet's evolution, focusing on long-range planning and coordination. It reviews new Working Group charters, sponsors the Internet Research Task Force, and approves the RFC Editor and IANA appointments.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains registries of protocol parameters such as TCP port numbers and MIME types, preventing conflicts in Internet implementations. The RFC Editor edits, formats, and publishes RFCs, maintaining the authoritative repository. The IETF Secretariat provides day-to-day logistical support, coordinating meetings, maintaining mailing lists, and providing tools for the community.
sections.plainLanguage: Several organizations support the IETF's work. ISOC provides money and legal help. The IESG makes decisions about standards. The IAB looks at big-picture Internet design. IANA keeps track of special numbers. The RFC Editor publishes standards. The Secretariat handles the paperwork and meetings.

sections.title: IETF Meetings and Working Groups
sections.content:
IETF face-to-face meetings are week-long gatherings held three times a year, primarily to energize Working Groups to complete their tasks and promote cross-fertilization between groups. Meetings are open to anyone who registers and pays the fee. Meetings provide wireless Internet access, a terminal room with power and ports, continental breakfasts and afternoon snacks, and a social event.

Newcomer training on Sunday afternoons covers IETF structure, the standards process, and practical details. The agenda is deliberately fluid, with changes announced near the meeting start to accommodate last-minute schedule conflicts. Working Group meetings are not drafting sessions; the real work happens on mailing lists before and after meetings.

A Working Group (WG) is fundamentally a mailing list with a bit of supervision. Anyone can join by subscribing; there are no membership requirements. Each WG has a charter defining its scope and goals, one or two chairs who manage discussions, and a focused list of deliverables. WGs operate on rough consensus, often determined by humming at meetings—chairs ask supporters to hum if they agree; disagreement is expressed by silence. Interim meetings between IETFs require Area Director approval and must allow fair access for all participants.

Birds of a Feather (BOF) meetings allow interested people to gauge support for a new Working Group. A BOF requires Area Director approval, and only two BOF meetings can be held on a topic before either forming a Working Group or dropping the initiative.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF meets three times a year for a week. Anyone can come if they register. Working Groups are groups of people (mostly on email lists) who work on specific topics. Each has a chair and rules about what it can do. If there's interest in a new topic, people have a BOF meeting to see if it's worth starting a new group.

sections.title: Internet Drafts and the Standards Process
sections.content:
Every RFC begins as an Internet Draft (I-D). Internet Drafts are tentative documents meant for comment and are automatically removed from repositories after six months. They have no formal status and are not specifications or standards. Authors submit drafts to the Internet Drafts administrator; Working Group drafts follow the naming convention "draft-ietf-[wg-name]-[topic]-[version].txt", while individual submissions follow "draft-[author-name]-[topic]-[version].txt".

The IETF publishes six kinds of RFCs: Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, Internet Standards (full standards), Informational, Experimental, and Historic. Only the first three are standards. Additionally, RFCs can be designated as Best Current Practice (BCP), For Your Information (FYI), or Standard (STD) documents.

To get a Working Group draft approved: the WG reaches consensus and conducts a "last call" for final comments, the WG chair submits it to the appropriate Area Director, the IESG conducts an IETF-wide last call (two weeks), and if approved, the RFC Editor publishes it as a Proposed Standard. The standard can later advance to Draft Standard (requiring two independent interoperable implementations) and then to Internet Standard (after several years and widespread deployment evidence).

IETF standards must clearly specify requirements using specific words. MUST and MUST NOT indicate absolute requirements; SHOULD and SHOULD NOT indicate strong recommendations subject to specific circumstances; MAY indicates optional features. All capitalized requirement keywords reference BCP 14. Standards must also include Security Considerations sections describing vulnerabilities, threats, and mitigation strategies.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFC starts as a draft that anyone can comment on. After months of discussion, it becomes a Proposed Standard if the IETF thinks it's good. It can later become a Draft Standard if people actually built two working versions of it, and eventually a full Standard if it's widely used. The words MUST, SHOULD, and MAY in standards have exact meanings that everyone uses.

sections.title: Participating in the IETF
sections.content:
The IETF operates through three main modes of participation: reading (reviewing Internet Drafts and commenting on them in Working Groups), implementing (writing programs that use current standards and reporting implementation problems), and writing (authoring or co-authoring Internet Drafts for the benefit of the Internet community, not for personal recognition).

Working Group mailing lists are the primary forum for technical discussion. All IETF decisions must gain consensus "on the list" after face-to-face meetings. Most WG lists are archived for public access. Some lists apply message-size limits to accommodate participants on slow connections; authors should post large documents as Internet Drafts and send only URLs to the list.

Many IETF participants are not vendors or academics but network operators who provide real-world operational expertise. The principle of rough consensus means that strongly held objections must be debated and addressed, not simply outvoted. This takes time but often results in better protocols.

Companies can support the IETF by avoiding proprietary standards, making patents available royalty-free to standards implementers, and becoming members of ISOC. Individual contributors can read the RFC 2026 (BCP 9) for detailed standards-process information, follow Working Group mailing lists, and attend IETF meetings.
sections.plainLanguage: You participate in the IETF by reading drafts and giving feedback, building working code with the standards, or writing your own drafts. Most work happens on email lists, but meetings help people connect and work out hard problems. Your opinion matters if you back it up with good technical reasoning.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 4677 is an Informational document published in September 2006. It was known as FYI 17, part of the For Your Information series of RFCs designed for introductory and broad-audience topics. The document obsoletes RFC 3160, an earlier version of "The Tao of IETF", and is itself obsoleted by RFC 6722.

This RFC represents a comprehensive snapshot of the IETF's organization and processes as they existed in 2006. While many details have evolved, the fundamental principles—rough consensus, running code, open participation, and volunteer-driven development—remain central to the IETF's mission and culture.
sections.plainLanguage: This document was written in 2006 to explain how the IETF works. It was later updated with a newer version. But the basic ideas—anyone can participate, consensus matters more than voting, working code proves your ideas—are still true today.
